slides.title: Head movement supplies depth through parallax
body: **Motion parallax** occurs because objects at different distances move across the retinal image by different amounts when the observer translates through space. Nearby objects usually shift more than distant objects for the same movement. Comparing those image changes provides information about depth even when only one eye is available.

Moving the head vertically before a jump changes the viewpoint of the landing surface and the gap. The brain can combine that image displacement with information about the head's movement. An image shift alone is ambiguous because it could result from the object moving, the observer moving, or both movements occurring together.

A self-generated movement can therefore become part of the sensory measurement. The animal does not merely wait for a better retinal picture; it changes the viewpoint that produces the picture. Head position, eye position, and the location of the landing edge determine which depth cues are available at the moment the jump is planned.

slides.title: Eye movements stabilize vision before a jump
body: The gap-jumping study used small head-mounted cameras to record both eyes while external cameras tracked the head and body. Eye rotations compensated for parts of the head movement, keeping gaze more stable than it would have been if the eyes had remained fixed within the skull throughout the decision period.

This stabilization did not eliminate the change in viewing position created by moving the head through space. The animal could therefore obtain movement-related depth information while reducing disruptive image rotation. Translating the viewpoint and rotating the eye have different effects on the retinal image, even when both occur during the same head movement.

Eye and head coordination also changed near the jump. Measuring both was necessary to identify the visual input available before takeoff. Tracking only the animal's body or only the pupil would omit part of the transformation between the physical landing surface, the changing retinal image, and the eventual movement across the gap.

slides.title: Parietal cortex turns visual estimates into actions
body: The **posterior parietal cortex** receives visual information through the dorsal stream and combines it with signals about body position and movement. Different regions contribute to selecting gaze targets, reaching toward objects, and shaping the hand for grasping. Their outputs communicate with frontal regions involved in preparing and controlling actions.

Reaching requires the target's location to be expressed relative to the moving limb. Grasping additionally requires the fingers to open by an appropriate amount and approach from a useful direction. The visual description needed for these actions changes continuously as the eyes, head, arm, and object move relative to one another.

Damage can impair these transformations while leaving object recognition relatively intact. A person may correctly judge that two objects differ in size yet fail to scale the opening of the hand before reaching. The impaired behavior concerns using visual dimensions to control an action, rather than failing to see that those dimensions differ.

slides.title: Suppressing V1 disrupts visually guided jumping
body: The researchers used **optogenetic suppression** to test whether visual cortex contributed to gap jumping. They expressed a light-sensitive channel in inhibitory interneurons, cells that reduce the activity of neighboring neurons. Illuminating those interneurons increased inhibition and temporarily reduced visual-cortical activity during the period when the mouse judged the gap.

Suppressing the relevant part of V1 impaired performance under binocular or monocular viewing conditions. The affected cortical region depended on the visual input available to the animal. This intervention tested a contribution of the cortical activity itself, beyond observing that neural responses might accompany successful jumps.

The source film compares trials with and without the suppression light. The animal still had to initiate a movement, cross the gap, and land on the platform. Recording where the jump ended separated a disruption of visually guided targeting from a description limited to whether the animal moved at all.

slides.title: Motion-sensitive cortex estimates trajectories
body: In primates, area **MT**, also called V5, contains many neurons sensitive to visual motion. Individual cells can prefer particular directions and speeds. Population activity therefore provides information about how image features move over time, rather than describing only which positions or orientations are occupied in a single moment.

Area **MST** receives motion-related input and responds to more complex movement patterns, including expansion and rotation. Such patterns occur when an observer moves through the environment. They can help distinguish a target's local motion from the broad displacement of image features caused by movement of the eyes, head, or body.

Damage involving motion-sensitive cortex can produce **akinetopsia**, difficulty experiencing continuous movement. An affected observer may identify an object's successive positions without perceiving the usual smooth motion between them. Detecting that an object has changed location and representing its trajectory are therefore related but separable functions within the visual system.

slides.title: Internal motion can bend an object's perceived path
body: The **double-drift illusion** combines two motions: a visible window moves through space while the texture inside it drifts in another direction. Observers can perceive the window traveling along a path that differs from its physical trajectory. Motion within the object changes the estimated position of the object containing it.

Steinberg and colleagues examined the illusion while observers tracked a moving fixation target. The target's movement kept the drifting stimulus relatively stable on the retina, yet the perceived trajectory could still deviate. The response therefore required considering information about eye movement together with the motion signals within the retinal image.

The illusion separates the physical path, retinal stimulation, and experienced path. These normally agree closely enough that their distinct contributions are difficult to notice. Here, combining the texture's drift with the window's motion shifted the position estimate over time, producing a systematic trajectory error rather than merely making the object difficult to see.

slides.title: Motion cortex carried the illusory trajectory signal
body: The double-drift study measured **BOLD fMRI**, a blood-oxygenation response related to local neural activity, while observers experienced different illusory paths. Several visual areas responded more strongly during the illusion than during a comparison condition. The researchers then asked whether patterns of activity contained information about which illusory trajectory was perceived.

Activity patterns in **hMT+**, the human motion-sensitive cortical complex, distinguished the illusory trajectories. Other measured visual regions did not provide the same successful readout. The result identified information within a regional population response rather than assuming that any increase in activity necessarily represented the object's perceived path.

Eye movements were recorded during scanning, and the trajectories could not be recovered from those eye-position measurements. The cortical result therefore was not explained by observers simply following different paths with their eyes. Retinal motion and information about gaze were combined within a representation carrying the systematically shifted trajectory.

slides.title: Gaze shifts alternate with stabilized viewing
body: Michaiel and colleagues recorded the eyes and head of mice pursuing crickets. When the head turned, the eyes often moved in the opposite direction, temporarily keeping gaze stable. The visual scene therefore moved less across the retina than would be predicted from the head rotation alone.

These stabilized periods were interrupted by rapid **saccades**, gaze shifts that moved the viewing direction toward a new location. During pursuit, noncompensatory eye movements helped bring gaze into alignment with the head as the animal targeted the cricket. The gaze sequence contained both compensation for movement and deliberate relocation of the visual sample.

A camera attached only to the body would combine these different phases into one apparent turn. Recording eye position revealed when retinal stimulation remained relatively stable and when it shifted rapidly. The changing pattern determined which part of the scene was sampled during each stage of the approach toward moving prey.

slides.title: Retinal motion and perceived motion can differ
body: An image can move across the retina because an object moved or because the eyes moved across a stationary scene. During a saccade across a page, the retinal image of the text shifts rapidly even though the words appear stationary. Interpreting motion therefore requires information about the cause of the image displacement.

A copy of an eye-movement command can inform sensory circuits that the retinal shift was self-generated. Signals from head movement and other senses contribute additional information about the observer's motion. Visual networks use these signals together with the pattern of image change to estimate which objects moved relative to the surrounding environment.

The converse also occurs during tracking: a pursued object can remain near the same retinal location while being perceived as moving through the world. Stable retinal position is therefore compatible with perceived motion when gaze changes appropriately. The estimated trajectory depends on combining retinal location over time with the changing direction of the eyes.

slides.title: Retinal motion channels predict eye reflexes
body: The **optokinetic reflex** stabilizes vision when a broad visual pattern moves across the retina. Direction-selective ganglion cells respond preferentially to particular directions of motion and supply information used to drive compensatory eye movements. The retinal input therefore carries an estimate of image motion before the stabilizing response is generated.

The mouse study compared ON direction-selective cells preferring opposite vertical directions. Their tuning was asymmetric and changed with contrast. Differences in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs, together with the firing threshold, contributed to these unequal outputs rather than producing two perfectly matched channels with reversed preferences.

Combining the retinal measurements with a central subtraction of competing directional outputs predicted vertical eye-movement trajectories across stimulus conditions. A change in the balance of the retinal channels could therefore alter the reflex's direction or time course. The behavioral response depended on how the brain compared their signals, not just whether any motion-sensitive cell fired.
transcript: The **optokinetic reflex** stabilizes vision when a broad visual pattern moves across the retina. Direction-selective ganglion cells respond preferentially to particular directions of motion and supply information used to drive compensatory eye movements. The retinal input therefore carries an estimate of image motion before the stabilizing response is generated.

The mouse study compared ON direction-selective cells preferring opposite vertical directions. Their tuning was asymmetric and changed with contrast. Differences in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs, together with the firing threshold, contributed to these unequal outputs rather than producing two perfectly matched channels with reversed preferences.

Combining the retinal measurements with a central subtraction of competing directional outputs predicted vertical eye-movement trajectories across stimulus conditions. A change in the balance of the retinal channels could therefore alter the reflex's direction or time course. The behavioral response depended on how the brain compared their signals, not just whether any motion-sensitive cell fired.

slides.title: A pursuing mouse coordinates its eyes and head
body: During cricket pursuit, a mouse must keep the target available while moving its own head and body. Simultaneous eye-camera and overhead recordings located the eyes relative to the head and the head relative to the arena. These measurements distinguished a change in eye rotation from an actual change in the direction of gaze.

The direction of each eye was estimated from pupil position and combined with head orientation. This produced a time-varying description of the animal's visual sampling during turns and approaches. The cricket's location could then be compared with the viewing direction as the distance between predator and prey decreased.

The eyes were not fixed cameras mounted on a moving body. Their compensatory rotations and rapid gaze shifts changed the image reaching the retina throughout the pursuit. A successful approach required the animal to obtain useful target information while the sensory surface collecting that information was itself continually moving.

slides.title: Optic flow changes as the observer moves
body: **Optic flow** is the pattern of image motion produced across the visual field as the observer moves relative to the environment. During forward travel, many visible features expand outward from a region near the direction of heading. Nearby surfaces usually produce faster image changes than surfaces farther away.

The flow also changes when the eyes rotate or the head turns. A broad rotation of the image can occur without the observer translating toward a new location. Estimating heading therefore requires distinguishing image changes caused by translation from those caused by rotation, using visual patterns and signals about the observer's own movements.

Motion-sensitive cortical areas analyze these larger patterns rather than only following one isolated feature. Expansion, contraction, and curved flow can provide information about approach and turning. The contribution of each pattern depends on where the observer looks and which surfaces occupy the visible scene at that moment.

slides.title: Human walkers stabilize gaze on chosen locations
body: Muller and colleagues measured eye position, body movement, and the three-dimensional environment while people walked naturally. These measurements allowed them to estimate the retinal motion created by real locomotion. The source recording combines the observer's changing view with information about gaze and body position during the walk.

When gaze remained on a chosen location, the eyes compensated for the body's forward movement. That compensation shaped the retinal flow across the surrounding scene. Motion near the fixated region differed from motion farther away, so the image pattern depended on both the environment's geometry and the observer's gaze behavior.

Different gaze directions changed the distribution of motion speeds and directions across the retina. Looking down toward the walking surface produced a different input from looking farther ahead or to one side. The visual system therefore receives a behavior-dependent distribution of motion signals rather than one fixed flow pattern determined by walking speed alone.

slides.title: Sparse motion can reveal a biological action
body: A moving person can be recognized from a small set of lights attached near major joints. Each individual point provides little information about a body, but their coordinated trajectories preserve the relationships among limbs. This is **biological motion**, movement whose organization can reveal the action of a living body.

Changing joint positions through time constrains which points belong together. Opposing arm and leg movements, bending knees, and the relative motion of shoulders and hips can specify walking without a visible outline or textured surface. The nervous system can recover structured form from the way sparse elements move together.

Regions around the posterior superior temporal sulcus contribute to processing such organized actions. Their responses differ from a simple detector for any moving dot. Recognizing the action requires integrating movements across body locations and time, while distinguishing their biological arrangement from an equally active but spatially scrambled set of trajectories.

slides.title: A moving scene evokes compensatory fly gaze
body: A fruit fly uses visual feedback to stabilize its head during movement. Cellini and colleagues presented moving patterns while comparing flies whose bodies could rotate with flies whose bodies were fixed. Cameras measured the head's response, separating movement of the head relative to the body from rotation of the entire animal.

The body-fixed flies made larger head movements in response to the same visual perturbation. Allowing the body to move changed the mechanical and sensory conditions under which the head stabilized gaze. A visual pattern therefore did not produce one invariant head response independently of the animal's other available movements.

The recordings preserve the original time course of the visual perturbation and resulting motion. Comparing the head relative to the room with the head relative to the body distinguishes two stabilization demands. The nervous system must coordinate them because the eyes are carried on a head that can move on an independently moving body.

slides.title: Body feedback damps visually driven head movement
body: **Mechanosensory feedback** reports physical movement or deformation through sensory structures in the body. In the fly experiment, signals generated by body motion reduced the size of the visually driven head response. This **damping** limited excessive movement that could otherwise destabilize gaze while the animal corrected a visual disturbance.

The researchers compared self-generated body movements with rotations imposed by a motor. The resulting head responses differed, indicating that feedback depended on the movement's motor context. A signal accompanying the animal's own turn was therefore not processed identically to a similar physical turn imposed from outside.

The source recording captures simultaneous body and head saccades against a stationary visual background. Coordinated movements relocate gaze without requiring the body and head to remain locked together. The visual and mechanosensory loops adjust different components of the movement while interacting through the head's changing position on the body.

slides.title: Cortical electrodes evoke localized light percepts
body: A **phosphene** is a perceived spot or region of light produced without light entering the eye at that location. Fernández and colleagues implanted a small electrode array in the occipital cortex of a blind participant. Electrical pulses could activate nearby neural tissue and produce visual percepts associated with particular stimulation sites.

The participant described the location and appearance of the evoked percepts. Different electrodes could produce percepts in different parts of visual space, allowing the investigators to map the available signals. Changing stimulation strength also altered properties such as detectability, making the stimulation parameters part of the information delivered to the visual system.

Some experiments recorded neural firing around the electrodes while stimulation was delivered. Neural activation and a reported phosphene were measured separately, because increased local firing did not guarantee a conscious light percept on every trial. A cortical interface therefore required both physiological measurements and the participant's report of the resulting visual experience.

body: In retinal degeneration, photoreceptors can die while some inner-retinal neurons remain. **Optogenetic restoration** introduces a light-sensitive protein into those surviving cells. Illumination can then change their membrane current directly, bypassing part of the lost photoreceptor pathway while retaining a route for signals to leave the retina and reach the brain.

The 2025 mouse study expressed channelrhodopsin variants in retinal ganglion cells of animals with severe photoreceptor degeneration. Light evoked action potentials in treated cells. A faster-closing ChRmine variant also improved performance in a light-avoidance test at a lower tested illumination than the other variants, linking channel properties to a measured behavior.

Closing speed and light sensitivity describe different aspects of the introduced channel. A channel that closes slowly can blur rapid changes, while one requiring intense light may fail under dim conditions. In the behavioral test, a change in preference between bright and dark compartments measured how the restored light signal influenced the animal’s location.

slides.title: Electrical patterns can convey a visual choice
body: A cortical prosthesis must deliver distinguishable patterns rather than simply produce any detectable sensation. In the intracortical study, stimulating different groups of electrodes produced patterns the participant learned to discriminate. A two-choice task associated particular stimulation patterns with responses, allowing the investigators to measure whether the delivered alternatives could be distinguished.

One task used a game display in which each direction corresponded to a particular electrode group. The participant pressed the matching response button after stimulation. The displayed game organized the trials; the experimentally conveyed information was the difference between the electrical patterns delivered to visual cortex.

Electrode positions did not translate one for one into visual pixels. Four neighboring electrodes could produce three perceived dots, while a larger group could produce a horizontal line. Mapping these actual percepts allowed researchers to select distinguishable patterns and teach the participant to use their differences as cues for the appropriate response.

slides.title: A camera can supply input to cortical stimulation
body: The study also used a camera mounted on eyeglasses to capture the scene. A processor transformed the camera image into a pattern of electrode commands, emphasizing selected spatial and temporal features. The stimulator then converted those commands into electrical pulses delivered through the implanted cortical array.

This pathway bypassed the usual optical-to-retinal conversion for the encoded information. The camera measured light, software selected and transformed features, and cortical electrodes activated neural tissue. The participant's remaining visual pathways and experience then determined how the resulting percepts could be used to perform the experimental task.

The transformation required a mapping between image features and electrode responses. An electrode did not function as an ordinary retinal photoreceptor with its natural connections preserved. The investigators first measured the available percepts and trained the participant to interpret selected patterns before testing camera-guided localization of simple high-contrast targets.

slides.title: Head scanning helps locate camera-encoded edges
body: Moving a camera across an edge changes which parts of its image are bright and dark. In the cortical-interface experiment, the participant used head scanning while the eyeglass camera supplied stimulation commands. Changes in the evoked percepts could then be compared with the direction of the self-generated head movement.

The participant localized the border between dark and light bars and pointed toward simple bright targets at different screen locations. These tasks tested whether the camera-to-cortex signal could support a spatial action. The participant's own movement helped convert a limited set of evoked signals into information about where a target lay.

Localization became faster with practice over the tested sessions. The improvement concerned using the interface's particular signals to guide a response. As in natural active vision, useful spatial information emerged from a sequence of samples combined with movement, although the camera, encoding algorithm, and cortical stimulation replaced several stages of the normal retinal pathway.

items.text: Activated pigment closes cyclic-GMP-dependent channels; hyperpolarization reduces calcium entry and glutamate release.
ON/OFF pathways, center-surround interactions, spectral comparisons, and synaptic timing create parallel visual signals.
Adaptation, surrounding contrast, contour completion, and motion integration can change appearance without matching changes in the stimulus.
Ventral networks contribute to recognition; dorsal networks transform visual estimates into gaze, reaching, grasping, and navigation.
Early retinal rerouting changes auditory-cortical visual responses; later visual experience can recalibrate existing pathways and actions.
Eye and head movements change retinal sampling and depth cues; neural interfaces can supply limited visual information through alternative input routes.
